subject: English
topic: Error Detection — Subject-Verb Agreement, Pronoun, Tense and Idiom Errors (W12 B1)

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) The news / (B) are very / (C) disturbing today / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'News' is an uncountable singular noun and always takes a singular verb. 'Are very disturbing' should be 'IS very disturbing.' Similar nouns: information, furniture, luggage, advice, knowledge — all singular. Trap: students confuse 'news' with plural (it ends in -s) but it has no singular 'new' counterpart; it is always singular.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) She is one of / (B) the most talented students / (C) that has ever studied / (D) at this university
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'One of the + superlative + plural noun + that/who' requires a PLURAL verb. The relative clause 'that has/have...' refers to the plural noun 'students' (not 'one'), so the verb must be 'have'. Correct: 'that HAVE ever studied.' SSC favourite: 'one of those writers who HAVE' (not 'has'). Trap: thinking the antecedent is 'one' (singular), which gives 'has' — but the relative clause modifies 'students', not 'one'.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) She is very / (B) much interested / (C) for learning / (D) new things
questions.explanation: C is correct. The correct preposition after 'interested' is 'IN', not 'for'. 'Interested IN learning new things.' Similarly: interested in mathematics, interested in sports. The preposition 'for' does not follow 'interested'. Trap: 'for' is used with other expressions (e.g., 'eager for', 'enthusiastic about') — but 'interested' specifically takes 'in'.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) An honest man / (B) never hesitates / (C) to speak / (D) a truth
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Speak the truth' is the correct idiomatic expression (definite article THE, not indefinite article 'a'). 'Truth' here refers to the universal concept of truthfulness/honesty — hence the definite article 'the'. 'A truth' would mean one specific true statement, which changes the meaning. Correct: 'to speak THE truth.' Trap: 'a truth' looks grammatically plausible but violates the fixed idiom.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) When I / (B) will reach / (C) the station, / (D) I will call you
questions.explanation: B is correct. In a time clause beginning with 'when', 'after', 'before', 'until', 'as soon as', the Simple Present tense is used (not Future). Correct: 'When I REACH the station, I will call you.' The future meaning is carried by the main clause ('I will call you'), not the 'when' clause. Trap: native speakers also sometimes say 'when I will reach' — but in formal grammar and SSC exams, 'when + Simple Present' is the rule.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) Between you / (B) and I, / (C) this project / (D) will be difficult
questions.explanation: B is correct. Prepositions (between, from, with, for, by, to) require an OBJECTIVE pronoun. 'Between you and I' is wrong; correct: 'Between you and ME.' Objective pronouns: me, him, her, us, them. Nominative (subject) pronouns: I, he, she, we, they. The hypercorrection 'between you and I' is common in speech but always wrong. SSC PYQ favourite. Trap: 'between you and I' sounds formal or educated to some students — but it violates pronoun case rules.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) Despite of / (B) working hard, / (C) he could not / (D) pass the examination
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Despite' is a preposition that directly takes a noun or gerund — it does NOT need 'of'. Correct: 'DESPITE working hard...' (not 'despite of'). Contrast: 'in spite of' = correct (in spite + of + noun); 'despite' = correct (no 'of'); 'despite of' = always wrong. Common confusion: students mix up 'despite' and 'in spite of'. Trap: 'despite of working' sounds like 'in spite of working' which is correct — but removing 'of' is required with 'despite'.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) Neither the principal / (B) nor the teachers / (C) was present / (D) at the meeting
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule for neither...nor / either...or: the verb agrees with the NEAREST subject. Here the nearest subject to the verb is 'teachers' (plural) → verb must be 'WERE' not 'was'. Correct: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers WERE present.' If it were 'Neither the teachers nor the principal was present' — then 'was' would be correct. Trap: students use 'was' (singular) thinking 'neither' controls the verb — but the proximity rule overrides.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) He said that / (B) he doesn't know / (C) nothing about / (D) the incident
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Doesn't know nothing' is a double negative — two negatives cancel to give a positive (he DOES know something). Correct English allows only one negative per clause. Options: either 'doesn't know ANYTHING about the incident' (negative verb + positive object) or 'knows NOTHING about the incident' (positive verb + negative object). Trap: double negatives are common in informal speech but always wrong in standard English grammar tested in SSC.

questions.stem: Find the segment with the grammatical error: (A) If I had / (B) studied harder, / (C) I would have / (D) pass the exam
questions.explanation: D is correct. Third conditional structure: 'If + had + V3, would have + V3'. The result clause requires 'would have PASSED', not 'would have pass' (base form). Correct: 'I would have PASSED the exam.' The pattern: If I had worked → I would have succeeded (both parts use perfect forms). Trap: students sometimes use the base verb after 'would have' because 'would + base verb' is correct for second conditional — but after 'would have', the past participle (V3) is required.
